overview: This file documents the U.S. response to the destructive April 21, 1935 Shinchiku–Taichu earthquake in Japanese-ruled Taiwan, together with a smaller earthquake reported in July. It combines initial casualty reports, formal condolences from President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull, Japanese acknowledgments, private appeals for American assistance, and exchanges between the State Department, White House, Navy Department, and American Red Cross over possible relief. Later material supplies detailed official figures—3,249 dead, 11,993 injured, 260,000 requiring relief—and describes extensive housing and railway damage, the disproportionate impact on Formosan Chinese, the survival of the Sun Moon Lake hydroelectric works, and military objections to abandoning a strategically defensible railway line.

subfiles.title: Initial report of the April 21 Taiwan earthquake
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consulate, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports the first casualty estimates and physical effects of the April 21 earthquake in central Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Maney reports an April 21 earthquake near Taichung killing an estimated 2,600, injuring 6,000, destroying Qingshui and burning Dajia; Taipei was undamaged, Americans safe.

subfiles.title: Roosevelt's condolences to Emperor Hirohito
subfiles.about: Extends the sympathy of the American people for the suffering and loss of life caused by the Taiwan disaster.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt sends Emperor Hirohito formal condolences, expressing American sympathy for Japan and those affected by the earthquake disaster.

subfiles.title: Hull informs the Tokyo embassy of condolence messages
subfiles.about: Notifies the embassy that Roosevelt and Hull have sent messages concerning the Taiwan disaster.
subfiles.summary: Hull reports Roosevelt telegraphed condolences to the Emperor and that he sent a similar message to Japan's foreign minister.

subfiles.title: Hull's condolences to Koki Hirota
subfiles.about: Expresses the American government's sorrow over the destruction of life and property in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Hull assures Foreign Minister Hirota of America's profound concern over the earthquake's loss of life and property damage.

subfiles.title: Hull forwards the Taihoku report to the American Red Cross
subfiles.about: Provides the American Red Cross with a copy of the consular earthquake telegram.
subfiles.summary: Hull forwards the Taihoku earthquake report to the Red Cross's McClintock, later dated April 25 despite ambiguous OCR.

subfiles.title: Hirota thanks Hull for American sympathy
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the American government's message of sympathy for the Taiwan catastrophe.
subfiles.summary: Hirota thanks Hull for America's magnanimous sympathy on behalf of the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: White House referral of the Andrews–Brunner appeal
subfiles.about: Refers a White House communication on Taiwan relief for immediate consideration and reply.
subfiles.summary: White House referral sends an appeal to State Department officials for immediate consideration and reply.

subfiles.title: Andrews and Brunner urge relief assistance
subfiles.from: Benjamin R. Andrews and Edmund de S. Brunner
subfiles.about: Urges an official expression of sympathy and an offer of emergency supplies and medical services.
subfiles.summary: Andrews and Brunner ask Roosevelt to add an official sympathy statement to the Red Cross offer, proposing tents and medical aid from Manila.

subfiles.title: World Peace Ways appeal to Hull
subfiles.from: Estelle M. Sternberger, World Peace Ways
subfiles.about: Calls on the U.S. government to relieve distress in the Japanese disaster area.
subfiles.summary: Sternberger expresses hope the administration will follow traditional sympathy policies, trusting the president and State Department to act.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Sternberger on Japanese relief capacity
subfiles.about: Explains that the Japanese Red Cross believes it can manage the emergency without American assistance.
subfiles.summary: Hull replies that Japan's Red Cross told its American counterpart it was confident it could handle the emergency itself.

subfiles.title: White House referral sheet for an unidentified communication
subfiles.about: Refers an unidentified White House communication to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: White House referral sheet directs an unidentified communication to the State Department, with circulation stamps but no reproduced content.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Swift's naval-relief proposal
subfiles.about: Forwards Swift's proposal for immediate consideration while sending the original telegram to the Navy Department.
subfiles.summary: Howe refers Swift's naval-relief telegram to State for consideration, noting it was also sent to the Navy Department.

subfiles.title: Swift proposes sending the fleet with relief supplies
subfiles.about: Asks the president to dispatch a naval fleet carrying relief supplies to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Swift argues a relief-laden fleet would be a powerful friendship gesture, contrasting it with North Pacific maneuvers and urging haste before Easter.

subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on Swift's proposal
subfiles.from: M. M. J., Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends against acting on Swift's naval-relief proposal because Japanese relief arrangements are sufficient.
subfiles.summary: Memo notes State asked Navy to delay pending discussion, since the Red Cross confirmed Japan could manage the emergency; recommends telling Swift no further action is needed.

subfiles.title: Hull rejects the need for Swift's proposed relief fleet
subfiles.about: Explains that Japanese relief agencies have the emergency under control and that formal condolences have already been sent.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Swift Japan's Red Cross is confident it can handle the emergency, noting Roosevelt's and Hull's sympathy messages to the Emperor and foreign minister.

subfiles.title: McClintock conveys Tokugawa's reply
subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese Red Cross president's statement that existing relief arrangements are sufficient.
subfiles.summary: McClintock sends Phillips Prince Tokugawa's reply to Grayson, thanking the Red Cross for sympathy but reporting Japanese relief arrangements appear sufficient.

subfiles.title: Andrews thanks Hull for the American response
subfiles.about: Expresses appreciation for the government's condolences and its handling of the Red Cross offer.
subfiles.summary: Andrews thanks Hull, writing for himself and Brunner, for reporting the actions taken, arguing such gestures build genuine international understanding.

subfiles.title: McClintock reports Grayson's offer to Tokugawa
subfiles.about: Provides the text of the American Red Cross offer of assistance sent to the Japanese Red Cross.
subfiles.summary: McClintock tells Phillips that Grayson cabled Tokugawa with sympathy, praise for Japan's Red Cross response, and an assistance offer, citing press deadlines for prompt action.

subfiles.title: Phillips approves Grayson's Red Cross message
subfiles.about: Approves the American Red Cross cable sent to Prince Tokugawa.
subfiles.summary: Phillips thanks McClintock for Grayson's message text, fully approving its contents and agreeing it was properly dispatched without delay.

subfiles.title: McClintock acknowledges the consular earthquake report
subfiles.about: Thanks Hull for supplying the Taihoku vice consul's report on the Formosa disaster.
subfiles.summary: McClintock acknowledges Hull's letter and enclosed Taihoku telegram, saying the Red Cross is pleased to add the information to its files.

subfiles.title: Eleanor Roosevelt asks about relief gestures
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Red Cross or Congress should make an additional gesture of friendship toward earthquake victims.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt asks Phillips what the Red Cross has done for Formosa's victims, suggesting consulting Grayson and wondering if Congress might act.

subfiles.title: Phillips explains the completed relief inquiries
subfiles.about: Reviews the condolences and relief offers already made and concludes that no further American action is appropriate.
subfiles.summary: Phillips quotes Grayson's offer and Tokugawa's sufficiency reply, recounts Roosevelt's and Hull's messages, and notes Grayson learned from the ambassador of about 5,000 deaths, concluding the U.S. had done all it properly could.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch on earthquake damage in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Taiwan Government-General's official casualty, relief, and property-damage figures.
subfiles.summary: Despatch counts 3,249 dead, mostly Formosan Chinese, 11,993 injured, and 260,000 needing relief; it tallies destroyed/damaged houses and ¥14 million losses, debates abandoning the damaged mountain railway over Army objections, and notes Sun Moon Lake and the Consulate were unharmed.

subfiles.title: July earthquake near Miaoli
subfiles.from: Garrels, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo, relaying Taihoku
subfiles.about: Reports a new earthquake in Hsinchu Province with 49 deaths and 134 injuries.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo relays a Taihoku report of a July 17 earthquake near Miaoli killing 49 and injuring 134, with no Americans involved.

interest: Shows disaster relief shaping U.S.-Japan diplomacy, with officials deferring to Japanese assurances over outside aid.
